title: Microbial community structure and functional gene profiles of drinking water treatment plant sludge in South Africa: An exploratory pilot study
content:
by Chimdi Mang Kalu, Memory Tekere

Microbial characterization of drinking water treatment plant (DWTP) sludge helps inform sludge management strategies and supports the development of disposal policies and procedures. In South Africa, the microbial composition of DWTP sludge remains poorly documented. This study characterised the microbial communities and functional gene profiles in sludge samples collected from three DWTPs in Gauteng, Limpopo, and Mpumalanga. A shotgun metagenomic approach was employed to provide a broad assessment of microbial taxa and functional gene categories, while physicochemical analyses were conducted in an ISO/IEC 17025-accredited laboratory. Most measured physicochemical parameters complied with relevant standards, although elevated turbidity and ammonia concentrations were observed in samples from all three plants, and fluoride exceeded the guideline value in one plant. Microbial sequences were assigned to three major taxonomic groups, namely Bacteria, Fungi, and Viruses. Across the sampled plants, Pseudomonadota (60–80%) and Actinomycetota (10–20%) were the predominant bacterial phyla, Ascomycota (30–80%) and Basidiomycota (18–30%) were the dominant fungal phyla, and Uroviricota accounted for 70–90% of viral sequences. Functional annotation identified six major gene categories, with metabolism-related functions representing approximately 55–70% of annotated genes and human disease-associated functions accounting for 10–25%. Redundancy analysis indicated associations between microbial and functional gene profiles and several physicochemical variables, including electrical conductivity, total dissolved solids, total hardness, total alkalinity, manganese, aluminium, iron, turbidity, and chloride.
